claims.text: The rapidly solidified initial alloy is a predominantly homogeneous metastable solid-solution matrix.
The initial alloy contains dispersed, incompletely developed intermetallic regions.
Heating in air at 600–800 °C stimulates diffusional segregation and phase transformation.
Elevated temperature accelerates atomic diffusion in the metastable solid solution.
During high-temperature oxidizing exposure, Mg segregates to grain boundaries and interfaces.
Mg segregation causes localized regions to transform into stable Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds preferentially nucleate MgO.
The proposed Mg-rich intermetallics have a higher affinity for oxygen.
Oxidation of the Mg-rich intermetallics produces a compact and adherent MgO scale.
The intermetallic-to-oxide transformation alters the surface chemical potential.
The MgO layer reduces local corrosion rates.
The MgO layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Thermally aged specimens will contain clearly segregated Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the as-cast state.
Thermally aged specimens will develop a thinner MgO surface layer relative to the as-cast state.
The MgO surface layer on thermally aged specimens will be more adherent than that on as-cast specimens.
Thermally aged specimens will exhibit lower corrosion rates than as-cast specimens.
Thermally aged specimens will exhibit greater high-temperature oxidation resistance than as-cast specimens.
The proposed pathway applies to Mg-containing HEAs below 6 g/cm³ when constituent-property differences favor intermetallic formation.
The pathway is expected only in temperature and time regimes where diffusion is active without complete homogenization or undesirable coarsening.

contradictions.description: The aged specimen is predicted to have a thinner MgO layer relative to an as-cast baseline described as lacking a developed surface oxide scale. Without specifying a subsequent identical oxidation exposure for both states, a developed aged scale cannot straightforwardly be thinner than an initially absent or undeveloped scale.
